title: Whole-String Glob Match
statement:
You get a string text and a glob pattern. In the pattern:

  • ? matches exactly one character, any character;
  • * matches any sequence of characters, including the empty one;
  • every other character matches only itself.

Return true if the pattern matches the whole of text, not just a part of it.

examples.why: The star takes "report" and the rest matches letter for letter.
"a?" covers only two characters, and the match has to use all of text.
If the star stops at the first "a", the pattern ends with "laz" left over. The star has to swallow "xayl" so that "a?" lands on "az".

hints: Without stars this is a plain left-to-right comparison. The star is the only hard part: how many characters should it take?

Let match(i, j) say whether text from i on matches pattern from j on. A star gives two choices: take no character (j + 1) or take one more character and stay on the star (i + 1). There are only (m+1)·(n+1) states.
Fill that table from the ends backwards, one row at a time. Or go greedy: remember the last star you saw, and on a mismatch let that star swallow one more character and retry from just after it.

explain.intuition:
Every character except * forces a one-to-one step. A star is a choice: it can end now, or eat one more character of text and stay a star. Trying all choices recursively explodes, but the state is only two positions, (i, j): "does text from i match pattern from j?" That gives a table of size (m+1)·(n+1), and each cell needs O(1) work.

There is also a neat greedy view. Only the last star seen matters: if a later mismatch happens, giving an earlier star more characters can never help more than giving the last star more, because the last star can absorb anything an earlier one could. So remember where the last star was and how much text it has eaten, and on a mismatch let it eat one more.
steps: Let dp[i][j] be true when text[i:] matches pattern[j:]. The answer is dp[0][0].
Base row: dp[m][n] = true, and dp[m][j] is true only if pattern[j:] is all stars.
For a star: dp[i][j] = dp[i][j+1] (the star is empty) or dp[i+1][j] (the star eats text[i]).
For ? or a matching letter: dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j+1]. Otherwise false.
Each row only reads the row below it, so two arrays of length n + 1 are enough.
pitfalls: Treating the match as "contains". "a?" does not match "abc": both strings must be used up.
Letting the star stop at the first chance, as in the third example. Without backtracking or a table, greedy-shortest fails.
Forgetting that an empty text still matches a pattern of only stars.

solutions.title: Try every split of each star
solutions.idea: Recurse on (i, j). A star tries both "stop here" and "take one more character". Correct, but the same states are explored again and again.

solutions.title: Table over two positions
solutions.idea: dp[i][j]: does text[i:] match pattern[j:]? Fill from the bottom row up, keeping only two rows.

solutions.title: Greedy with the last star
solutions.idea: Match forward. On a star, remember its position and where text was. On a mismatch, let the last star eat one more character and resume right after it.
solutions.time: O(m·n) worst, usually near O(m + n)

followups: Why is it safe for the greedy version to forget every star except the last one?
Add a character class like [abc] to the pattern. Which version adapts most easily?
